lessons.title: Scalars, vectors and resolving forces
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Distinguish scalar and vector quantities and add vectors by the triangle or parallelogram rule
Resolve a vector into perpendicular components and recombine components into a resultant
Solve simple problems on resultant forces and relative velocity
reviewNotes: Vector product/scalar product are not included; check whether the syllabus asks for them at this stage.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Scalars and vectors
blocks.md:
A **scalar** has magnitude only (mass, time, distance, speed, energy, temperature). A **vector** has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum).

Vectors add by the **triangle rule** (head to tail) or the **parallelogram rule**. The result is the **resultant**. Two vectors at 90° give a resultant of size √(a² + b²).

blocks.title: Resolving a vector
blocks.md:
A vector F at angle θ to the x-axis has components **F_x = F cos θ** along x and **F_y = F sin θ** along y. Conversely F = √(F_x² + F_y²) and tan θ = F_y/F_x.

To add several vectors: resolve each into x and y components, add the components in each direction separately, then recombine.

blocks.caption: Resolving a force F into components along the axes.
blocks.alt: A force vector at angle theta to the horizontal with dashed horizontal and vertical components labelled F cos theta and F sin theta.

blocks.title: Method for a resultant
blocks.md:
1. Draw a clear sketch and choose axes (often along and perpendicular to the motion or slope).
2. Resolve each vector into components.
3. Add the x components and the y components separately (take care with signs).
4. Find the magnitude with Pythagoras and the direction with tan θ.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using cos for the component opposite the angle: the component **adjacent** to the angle uses cos, the opposite one uses sin.
- Adding magnitudes instead of vectors (3 N + 4 N is not always 7 N).
- A calculator in radian mode when the angle is in degrees.
- Forgetting to give a direction with the answer.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Resolving a force
blocks.statement: A 50 N force acts at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Resultant of two forces
blocks.statement: Two ropes pull a stuck vehicle: 30 N due east and 40 N due north. Find the resultant.
steps: The forces are at right angles: R = √(30² + 40²) = √2500 = 50 N.
Direction: tan θ = 40/30, so θ = 53.1° north of east.

lessons.title: Motion in a straight line
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define displacement, velocity and acceleration and use the equations of uniformly accelerated motion
Interpret displacement–time and velocity–time graphs (gradient and area)
Analyse free fall under gravity (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
reviewNotes: g = 9.8 m s⁻² is used; some Cameroonian schools use 10 m s⁻² — check the board's preference.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Quantities and graphs
blocks.md:
**Velocity** = rate of change of displacement; **acceleration** = rate of change of velocity (a vector, unit m s⁻²).

On a displacement–time graph the **gradient** is velocity. On a velocity–time graph the **gradient** is acceleration and the **area** under the graph is displacement.

blocks.title: Equations for constant acceleration (suvat)
blocks.md:
With u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = displacement:

- v = u + at
- s = ½(u + v)t
- s = ut + ½at²
- v² = u² + 2as

They apply **only when a is constant**. Choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent.

blocks.caption: Velocity–time graph of a minibus: the gradient gives acceleration and the area gives distance.
blocks.alt: A trapezium-shaped velocity time graph rising to 12 metres per second at 4 seconds, flat until 10 seconds, then falling to zero at 14 seconds.

blocks.title: Free fall
blocks.md:
Near the Earth's surface, with air resistance neglected, all objects fall with the same acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward. For an object thrown up, take up as positive so a = −9.8 m s⁻².

At the highest point v = 0 (but a is still −9.8 m s⁻²). Time up = time down, if it returns to its starting height.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the suvat equations when the acceleration is not constant (use graphs instead).
- Mixing signs: a ball thrown up and then falling has a negative acceleration throughout.
- Confusing distance and displacement, or speed and velocity.
- Reading the area under a v–t graph below the axis as positive: it is negative displacement.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Accelerating car
blocks.statement: A taxi leaves a stop in Douala and reaches 20 m/s in 8.0 s with constant acceleration. Find the acceleration and the distance covered.

blocks.title: Example 2 — A stone thrown upward
blocks.statement: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 19.6 m/s. Find the maximum height and the time to reach it (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
steps: Take up as positive: u = 19.6, a = −9.8, and v = 0 at the top.
v = u + at gives 0 = 19.6 − 9.8t, so t = 2.0 s.
blocks.answer: H = 19.6 m, time to top = 2.0 s

lessons.title: Projectile motion
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Treat horizontal and vertical motions independently for a projectile
Calculate time of flight, range and maximum height for a launch at an angle
Solve problems on horizontal launch from a height
reviewNotes: Range and height formulas rely on level ground; air resistance is ignored.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Independence of motion
blocks.md:
A **projectile** moves under gravity only (air resistance neglected). Its horizontal and vertical motions are **independent**:

- horizontal: constant velocity, a = 0, so x = u_x t
- vertical: constant acceleration g downward.

The path is a **parabola**.

blocks.title: Launch at speed u, angle θ above the horizontal
blocks.md:
Components: u_x = u cos θ, u_y = u sin θ.

- Time of flight (level ground): T = 2u sin θ / g
- Maximum height: H = u² sin² θ / 2g
- Range: R = u² sin 2θ / g (maximum at θ = 45°)

The range formula holds only if landing at the launch height.

blocks.caption: Path of a ball launched at 20 m/s at 30°: height y against horizontal distance x.
blocks.alt: A parabolic curve starting at the origin, rising to about 5 metres at 17 metres and returning to the ground at 35 metres.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Resolve the initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
2. Use the vertical motion (suvat with a = −g) to find the time.
3. Use the horizontal motion x = u_x t with that time.
4. For the final velocity, combine v_x and v_y with Pythagoras.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the range formula when the projectile lands at a different height.
- Applying gravity to the horizontal motion.
- Taking the velocity at the top as zero: only the vertical component is zero there.
- Using the total speed in the suvat equations instead of one component.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Ball kicked at an angle
blocks.statement: A footballer in Bamenda kicks a ball at 20 m/s at 30° above the ground. Find the time of flight, the range and the maximum height (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Horizontal launch
blocks.statement: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a 45 m cliff. How long does it take to land, how far from the base, and what is its speed on landing?

lessons.title: Newton's laws, friction and free-body diagrams
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State Newton's three laws and use F = ma for a body and for connected bodies
Draw free-body diagrams and resolve forces along and perpendicular to a slope
Use friction f ≤ μN and explain terminal velocity
reviewNotes: Static versus kinetic friction: the lesson uses a single μ; check whether the syllabus distinguishes them.
Some boards phrase the second law as F = dp/dt; both forms are given.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Newton's laws
blocks.md:
1st law: a body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a **resultant force** acts on it.

2nd law: the resultant force is the rate of change of momentum; for constant mass **F = ma** (F in newtons, a in m s⁻²). 1 N is the force giving 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².

3rd law: if A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces act on **different bodies** and are of the same kind.

blocks.title: Method for dynamics problems
blocks.md:
1. Isolate one body and draw a **free-body diagram**: weight mg, normal reaction N, tension, friction, applied forces.
2. Choose axes (along and perpendicular to the motion).
3. Along the motion: resultant force = ma. Perpendicular to it: forces balance.
4. For connected bodies write an equation for each body, then solve together.

blocks.caption: Forces on a box on a slope (free-body diagram).
blocks.alt: A box on an inclined plane with arrows for weight vertically down, normal reaction perpendicular to the plane and friction up the slope.

blocks.title: Friction and slopes
blocks.md:
Friction opposes the relative motion; the maximum (limiting) value is **f = μN** where μ is the coefficient of friction and N the normal reaction.

On a slope of angle θ: weight component down the slope = mg sin θ; perpendicular to the slope = mg cos θ, so N = mg cos θ.

blocks.title: Terminal velocity
blocks.md: A falling object in air meets a drag force that grows with speed. The resultant force and acceleration fall until the drag equals the weight; then a = 0 and the speed is constant: the **terminal velocity**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Calling weight and the normal reaction an action–reaction pair: they act on the same body. The reaction to the weight is the gravitational pull of the body on the Earth.
- Writing N = mg on a slope: it is mg cos θ.
- Forgetting friction acts up the slope when the body slides down.
- Using a mass in newtons or a weight in kilograms.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Block with friction
blocks.statement: A 5.0 kg crate is pulled along a rough floor by a horizontal force of 30 N. Friction is 10 N. Find its acceleration.
steps: Resultant force along the floor = 30 − 10 = 20 N.
blocks.answer: a = 4.0 m s⁻² in the direction of the pull

blocks.title: Example 2 — Sliding down a slope
blocks.statement: A 10 kg box slides down a 30° slope with μ = 0.20. Find its acceleration (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
steps: Perpendicular to the slope: N = mg cos 30° = 10 × 9.8 × 0.866 = 84.9 N.
Friction f = μN = 0.20 × 84.9 = 17.0 N up the slope. Down-slope component of weight = mg sin 30° = 49.0 N.
blocks.answer: a = 3.2 m s⁻² down the slope

lessons.title: Momentum, impulse and collisions
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define momentum and impulse and apply the conservation of linear momentum
Distinguish elastic and inelastic collisions using kinetic energy
Use impulse = force × time = change of momentum, including F–t graphs
reviewNotes: Collisions in two dimensions are not covered; check the syllabus.
Elastic head-on collision speeds (general formula) are not derived here.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Momentum and impulse
blocks.md:
**Linear momentum** p = mv (a vector, unit kg m s⁻¹ or N s). **Impulse** = force × time of contact = FΔt = Δp, the change of momentum. On a force–time graph the **area** under the curve is the impulse.

Newton's second law in its general form: F = Δp/Δt.

blocks.title: Conservation of momentum
blocks.md:
In a closed system (no external resultant force) **total momentum before = total momentum after**: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

Momentum is a vector: choose a positive direction and give velocities signs. It is conserved in **all** collisions and explosions.

blocks.caption: Two trolleys before and after a perfectly inelastic collision.
blocks.alt: A 2 kilogram trolley moving at 3 metres per second and a stationary 1 kilogram trolley before the collision, then a 3 kilogram combined body at 2 metres per second after.

blocks.title: Elastic and inelastic collisions
blocks.md:
In an **elastic** collision total kinetic energy is also conserved (the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation). In an **inelastic** collision some kinetic energy is changed to heat, sound or deformation; if the bodies stick together the loss is the greatest ('perfectly inelastic').

Total energy is always conserved.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting that momentum is a vector: a ball bouncing back from a wall has a change of momentum m(v + u), not m(v − u).
- Saying kinetic energy is conserved in every collision: only in elastic ones.
- Mixing units (grams with kg).
- Using the wrong sign for a body moving in the negative direction.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Trolleys that stick
blocks.statement: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Find their common speed and the kinetic energy lost.
steps: Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s. After: (2.0 + 1.0)v = 6.0, so v = 2.0 m/s.
KE before = ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J; KE after = ½ × 3.0 × 2.0² = 6.0 J.
Energy lost = 9.0 − 6.0 = 3.0 J (to heat and sound).
blocks.answer: v = 2.0 m/s; 3.0 J of kinetic energy is lost

blocks.title: Example 2 — Ball and wall
blocks.statement: A 0.15 kg ball hits a wall at 20 m/s and rebounds at 15 m/s. The contact lasts 0.010 s. Find the impulse and the average force.
steps: Take the rebound direction as positive: change of momentum = 0.15 × 15 − 0.15 × (−20) = 2.25 + 3.00 = 5.25 N s.
F = impulse/time = 5.25 ÷ 0.010 = 525 N, directed away from the wall.
blocks.answer: Impulse 5.25 N s; average force 525 N

lessons.title: Work, energy and power
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate work done by a constant force, including at an angle to the displacement
Use kinetic energy ½mv² and gravitational potential energy mgh with conservation of energy
Calculate power and efficiency, including P = Fv
reviewNotes: Bars figure uses m = 2.0 kg and h = 10 m: mgh = 2.0 × 9.8 × 10 = 196 J.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Work, energy and power
blocks.md:
**Work** done by a force = force × displacement in the direction of the force: **W = Fs cos θ** (joule). **Energy** is the capacity to do work. **Power** is the rate of doing work, P = W/t (watt, 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹).

Work done by the resultant force equals the change in kinetic energy (the **work–energy theorem**).

blocks.title: Key formulae
blocks.md:
- Kinetic energy: E_k = ½mv²
- Gravitational potential energy (near the surface): ΔE_p = mgΔh
- Power: P = W/t = Fv (for a force along the velocity)
- Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (× 100 %)

When only gravity does work (no friction), E_k + E_p stays constant.

blocks.caption: A 2.0 kg object falling 10 m: energy at the top, halfway and at the bottom (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
blocks.alt: A bar chart showing 196 joules of potential energy at the top, 98 joules each of kinetic and potential energy halfway, and 196 joules of kinetic energy at the bottom.

blocks.title: Conservation of energy
blocks.md:
Energy is never created or destroyed; it changes form. Friction and air resistance convert mechanical energy to thermal energy, which is not 'lost' but no longer useful.

For a body falling through height h from rest with no friction: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A force perpendicular to the motion (for example the normal reaction, or the tension on a circular path) does **no work**.
- Forgetting the cos θ when the force is at an angle.
- Mixing kW h with J: 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
- Saying power is energy (it is energy per second).

blocks.title: Example 1 — A pump
blocks.statement: A pump raises 120 kg of water each minute through 15 m. Its efficiency is 60 %. Find the useful power and the power input (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
steps: Useful energy per minute = mgh = 120 × 9.8 × 15 = 17 640 J.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Roller coaster
blocks.statement: A car starts from rest at the top of a frictionless track 20 m above the bottom. Find its speed at the bottom (g = 9.8).
steps: Loss of potential energy = gain of kinetic energy: mgh = ½mv².

lessons.title: Uniform circular motion
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use angular displacement in radians, angular velocity ω, period T and frequency f
Explain why a body moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates, and use a = v²/r and F = mv²/r
Identify the force providing the centripetal force in simple situations
reviewNotes: Banked tracks and conical pendulum are not included; check the syllabus.
Use of 'centrifugal force' in the board's mark scheme should be checked.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Angular quantities
blocks.md:
An angle in **radians** = arc length ÷ radius (2π rad = 360°). **Angular velocity** ω = Δθ/Δt (rad s⁻¹). Period T = time for one revolution; frequency f = 1/T.

**ω = 2π/T = 2πf** and the linear speed on a circle of radius r is **v = ωr**.

blocks.title: Centripetal acceleration and force
blocks.md:
A body moving at constant speed in a circle has a velocity that keeps changing direction, so it **accelerates**. The acceleration points to the **centre**: a = v²/r = ω²r.

The resultant force towards the centre (centripetal force) is **F = mv²/r = mω²r**. It is not a new force: it is provided by tension, friction, gravity, a normal reaction…

items.text: force and acceleration point to the centre

blocks.caption: Uniform circular motion: the velocity is tangential; the resultant force and acceleration point to the centre.
blocks.alt: A circle with a body on it, an arrow along the tangent for velocity and an arrow towards the centre for force and acceleration.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Draw the free-body diagram of the body and identify the forces pointing to the centre.
2. The resultant towards the centre equals mv²/r.
3. Convert rpm to rad s⁻¹: multiply by 2π/60.
4. Remember: if the centripetal force vanishes the body moves off along the **tangent**, not outward.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- 'Centrifugal force' is not a real force acting on the body; do not add it to the free-body diagram.
- Using degrees in v = ωr: ω must be in rad s⁻¹.
- Saying the acceleration is zero because the speed is constant.
- Forgetting that the centripetal force does no work (it is perpendicular to the motion).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Car on a bend
blocks.statement: A 1200 kg car takes a flat circular bend of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. Find the centripetal force and the least coefficient of friction needed (g = 9.8).
steps: F = mv²/r = 1200 × 15²/50 = 5400 N, provided by friction between tyres and road.
Friction limit: μmg ≥ mv²/r, so μ ≥ v²/(rg) = 225/(50 × 9.8) = 0.46.

blocks.title: Example 2 — A spinning rotor
blocks.statement: A rotor turns at 3000 revolutions per minute. Find ω, the speed of a point 0.10 m from the axis, and its acceleration.

lessons.title: Gravitational fields and orbits
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — mechanics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State Newton's law of gravitation and define gravitational field strength
Derive and use orbital speed and period for circular orbits, including the geostationary orbit
Use gravitational potential and calculate escape speed
reviewNotes: Constants used: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, M_E = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, R_E = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. The geostationary period is taken as 24 h (the exact sidereal day is 23 h 56 min).
Gravitational potential may be placed in Upper Sixth by some schools; check the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Law and field
blocks.md:
**Newton's law**: two point masses attract with a force **F = GMm/r²** along the line joining them (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).

**Gravitational field strength** g = force per unit mass = GM/r², directed towards the mass M. At the Earth's surface it is about 9.8 N kg⁻¹ (= m s⁻²). Outside a spherical body, the mass acts as if concentrated at its centre.

blocks.title: Circular orbits
blocks.md:
For a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r the gravitational force provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r. So **v = √(GM/r)** and **T = 2πr/v**, giving **T² = (4π²/GM) r³** (Kepler's third law).

The mass of the satellite cancels: every satellite at the same radius has the same speed.

blocks.caption: A satellite in a circular orbit: gravity provides the centripetal force.
blocks.alt: The Earth at the centre, a circular orbit, a satellite and an arrow towards the Earth's centre labelled F.

blocks.title: Potential and escape speed
blocks.md:
**Gravitational potential** V = −GM/r (J kg⁻¹): work done per unit mass to bring a mass from infinity (V = 0 at infinity); it is negative. A mass m has potential energy −GMm/r.

To escape from the surface the kinetic energy must be at least GMm/R: **v_esc = √(2GM/R)** ≈ 11 km s⁻¹ for the Earth. A **geostationary** satellite has T = 24 h, orbits above the equator, and stays above one point.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the height above the surface as r: r is measured from the **centre** (r = R + h).
- Thinking astronauts are 'beyond gravity': in orbit they are in free fall, so they feel weightless.
- Forgetting that g varies as 1/r² (doubling r divides g by 4).
- Mixing km and m in GM/r.

blocks.title: Example 1 — g above the Earth
blocks.statement: Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, M_E = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and R_E = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, find g at the surface and at a height of one Earth radius above it.
steps: At a height R above the surface, r = 2R, so g is divided by 2² = 4: 9.77/4 = 2.44 m s⁻².
blocks.answer: 9.77 m s⁻² at the surface, 2.44 m s⁻² at height R

blocks.title: Example 2 — A low satellite
blocks.statement: A satellite orbits 400 km above the Earth (same data). Find its speed and period.
